What comes next in the alphanumeric series: A1, B3, C5, D7, ?

(A) E9 (next letter, +2 numbers)
(B) E8 (number under-counted)
(C) F9 (letter over-counted)
(D) E11 (number over-counted)
cards.back:
(A) E9 (next letter, +2 numbers)

Series & Sequences — DOUBLE PATTERN: LETTERS go A → B → C → D → E (+1 each step in alphabet). NUMBERS go 1 → 3 → 5 → 7 → 9 (+2 each step, odd-number sequence). So next term = E9. KEY METHOD for compound series: (1) split into letter-component and number-component. (2) find each pattern independently. (3) combine. ALPHABET POSITIONS: A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4, E=5. COMMON COMPOUND PATTERNS: (a) consecutive letters + odd numbers: A1, B3, C5, ... (b) skip-one letters + squares: A1, C4, E9, G16... (c) reverse alphabet + Fibonacci: Z1, Y1, X2, W3, V5... PRACTICE — VARIANT: A2, C4, E8, G16 (letters skip-one, numbers double); A1, B4, D9, G16 (letters jump by Fibonacci, numbers are squares). PYQ FREQUENCY: alphanumeric series is a top SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk, RRB NTPC pattern — 1-2 per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests systematic decomposition of compound sequences.

(B) 24M (number error pattern off) (option here)
(C) 32K (letter error wrong skip) (option here)

cards.back:
(A) 32M (numbers double, letters skip-three)

Series & Sequences — DOUBLE PATTERN: NUMBERS double each step: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 (× 2 progression, geometric). LETTERS skip 3 places (A, D, G, J, M; positions 1, 4, 7, 10, 13). Each step + 3. So next = 32M. KEY ALPHABET-POSITION MEMORY: A=1, D=4, G=7, J=10, M=13, P=16, S=19, V=22, Y=25. SHORTCUT for skip-3: every 3rd letter starting from A. KEY METHOD: (1) ISOLATE the number sequence. (2) ISOLATE the letter sequence. (3) Find each independently. EXAMINER VARIATIONS: numbers can be Fibonacci (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8...), prime (2, 3, 5, 7, 11), squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25), cubes (1, 8, 27, 64), or factorials (1, 2, 6, 24, 120). Letter can be skip-1, skip-2, skip-3, reverse, vowels-only, etc. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 alphanumeric series Qs per SSC CGL Tier 1; common in IBPS Clerk Pre. EXAM TIP: a term-by-term DIFFERENCE (or RATIO) check often reveals the pattern in seconds.

Series & Sequences — TRIPLE-COMPONENT PATTERN. Decompose: First letter: B(2) → D(4) → G(7) → K(11) → ? Differences: +2, +3, +4 → next +5 → 11+5 = 16 = P. Number: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 (×2). Last letter (relative to first letter): each term has the LAST LETTER one MORE than the FIRST: B2C (B+1=C), D4F (D+2=F)... wait, let me re-examine. Actually: B2C has +1; D4F has +2; G8I has +2; K16L has +1; pattern not clean — but most consistent: each term's LAST LETTER = FIRST LETTER + (term-number−1) so 5th term: P + 1 = Q. So answer: P32Q. KEY METHOD: when faced with three-letter alphanumeric, separately track each letter sequence + the number. EXAM TRAP: students get distracted by middle number and forget last letter. SHORTCUT: when puzzles look complex, check FIRST and LAST letter independently. PYQ ANGLE: triple-component series in CAT, advanced IBPS PO Mains. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests systematic decomposition; rewards persistence.

Identify the pattern: Z26, Y25, X24, W23, ?

(A) V22 (reverse alphabet position)
(B) V23 (number off by one)
(C) U22 (alphabet jumped extra)
(D) V21 (number under-counted)
cards.back:
(A) V22 (reverse alphabet position)

Series & Sequences — PATTERN: REVERSE ALPHABET + matching POSITION NUMBER. Z is the 26th letter (or 1st from end), Y is 25th, X is 24th, W is 23rd, V is 22nd. Each term decrements both letter AND number by 1. KEY ALPHABET-POSITION TABLE (memorize for quick recall): A=1/Z=26, B=2/Y=25, C=3/X=24, D=4/W=23, E=5/V=22, F=6/U=21, G=7/T=20, H=8/S=19, I=9/R=18, J=10/Q=17, K=11/P=16, L=12/O=15, M=13/N=14. SHORTCUT FORMULA: position from start + position from end = 27. So if you know A=1, Z=27−1 = 26 ✓; if N=14, M=14, both near middle (M=13, N=14, sum 27 ✓). USEFUL for problems like 'opposite letter pairs sum to 27'. EXAM-FAVORITE: problems where you need to identify a 'mirror letter' or convert between forward and reverse positions. PYQ FREQUENCY: reverse-alphabet series is a SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk Pre staple — 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests directional flexibility + alphabet-position fluency.

Series & Sequences — DUAL PATTERN. Numbers: 1 → 4 → 9 → 16 → 25 — these are PERFECT SQUARES (1², 2², 3², 4², 5²). Letters: A(1) → D(4) → G(7) → J(10) → M(13) — increment of +3 each step. NEXT TERM: 5² = 25; 13th letter = M → 25M. KEY: PERFECT SQUARE recognition is fundamental: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144, 169, 196, 225, 256, 289, 324, 361, 400 (squares of 1-20). When you see numbers from this list, IMMEDIATELY check if it's a square sequence. SAMPLE SQUARE PATTERNS in alphanumeric: A1, C4, E9, G16 (skip-one letters + squares); B1, D4, G9, K16 (Fibonacci-letter + squares); A1, B4, D9, G16 (positions 1, 2, 4, 7 = jumps +1, +2, +3 — triangular gaps). EXAM TIP: 'is this a square' check is often the fastest way to crack a numeric pattern. CUBE PATTERNS too — 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000. PYQ FREQUENCY: square/cube-based number sequences in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Pre 1-2× per paper.

cards.back:

Series & Sequences — DUAL PATTERN with INCREASING GAPS. Letters: A(1) → C(3) → F(6) → J(10) → O(15). Differences in letter positions: +2, +3, +4, +5 (next +5 → 15 = O). Numbers: 5 → 8 → 12 → 17 → 23. Differences: +3, +4, +5, +6 (next +6 → 17+6 = 23). So answer: O23. KEY METHOD: when both letter and number sequences have INCREASING GAPS, track each sequence's differences-of-differences. Triangular gap progression (+1 each step) is common. INSIGHT: triangular numbers (1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, ...) — formula T(n) = n(n+1)/2. The letter positions A, C, F, J, O are exactly T(1)=1, T(2)=3, T(3)=6, T(4)=10, T(5)=15. SHORTCUT: when gaps are +2, +3, +4, +5,... think TRIANGULAR PATTERN. EXAM TRAP: students guess +5 each step (constant gap) or just the next letter — both wrong. PYQ FREQUENCY: increasing-gap series in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS PO 1× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests difference-of-difference analysis; rewards mathematical pattern-spotting.

PYQ FREQUENCY: combined geometric-arithmetic patterns in IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B, CAT — moderately common. (A) O (gaps: +2, +3, +4, +5)
(B) N (a smaller jump letter)
(C) M (another option letter)
(D) P (a larger jump letter)
cards.back:
(A) O (gaps: +2, +3, +4, +5)

Series & Sequences — PATTERN: increasing gap by 1 each time. A → C (gap +2) → F (gap +3) → J (gap +4) → ? (gap +5). Position-wise: A=1, C=3, F=6, J=10, NEXT = 10+5 = 15 = O. DIFFERENCES SERIES: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6... (arithmetic progression of gaps). KEY METHOD — when a series doesn't have a constant gap: (1) compute differences. (2) check if differences themselves form a pattern (constant, arithmetic, geometric). (3) extend the differences and add to the last term. SAMPLE PATTERNS: (a) constant +2: A, C, E, G... (b) +1, +2, +3...: A, B, D, G, K, P (triangular gaps). (c) Fibonacci gaps: A, B, D, G, M, V (1, 2, 3, 5, 8...). (d) geometric: A, B, D, H, P (×2 gaps). PYQ FREQUENCY: increasing-gap series is a top SSC CGL trick — 1 per Tier 1 paper; mixed alphabetical/numerical in IBPS PO Reasoning.

cards.front:
Which letter comes next: Z, X, V, T, ?

(A) R (reverse skip-one)
(B) S (just one letter back)
(C) Q (a deeper jump back)
(D) U (forward direction now)
cards.back:
(A) R (reverse skip-one)

Series & Sequences — PATTERN: REVERSE ALPHABET, skipping one letter each time. Z=26 → X=24 (gap −2) → V=22 (gap −2) → T=20 (gap −2) → R=18 (gap −2). KEY: each step subtracts 2 in alphabetical position. SHORTCUT: when you see Z, Y, X, W, V... think 'reverse alphabet'; if every-other-letter, it's '−2 in position'. ALPHABET REVERSE POSITIONS: Z=1 (or 26), Y=2 (or 25), X=3 (or 24), ... A=26 (or 1). When tackling reverse problems, use the BACK-TO-FRONT positions: Z is the '1st from end', X is '3rd from end', etc. EXAM TRAP: students confuse forward (A→Z) and backward (Z→A) numbering. PRACTICE: Z X V T R P N L J H F D B — full reverse skip-one. PYQ FREQUENCY: reverse-direction series Qs in SSC, IBPS, SBI 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests directional flexibility + pattern recognition.

cards.front:
Find the missing term in the series: AZ, BY, CX, DW, ?

(A) EV (forward + reverse pair)
(B) FU (skipped a letter pair)
(C) EW (wrong second letter)
(D) DV (wrong first letter)
cards.back:
(A) EV (forward + reverse pair)

Series & Sequences — PATTERN: each term has TWO letters: (1) FIRST letter goes A → B → C → D → E (forward in alphabet, +1). (2) SECOND letter goes Z → Y → X → W → V (backward, −1). So the next pair is E + V = EV. INSIGHT: this is a 'PAIRED-DIRECTION' pattern — first letter increments, second letter decrements. POSITION ARITHMETIC: A(1)+Z(26) = 27; B(2)+Y(25) = 27; C(3)+X(24) = 27; D(4)+W(23) = 27. EVERY pair sums to 27! So the next pair must be E(5) + V(22) = 27 ✓. RELATED PATTERN: 'AZ' is the FIRST + LAST letter; 'BY' is the SECOND + SECOND-LAST, etc. — known as 'opposite-letter pairs'. OPPOSITE-LETTER MEMORIZATION: A↔Z, B↔Y, C↔X, D↔W, E↔V, F↔U, G↔T, H↔S, I↔R, J↔Q, K↔P, L↔O, M↔N. Each pair sums to 27. PYQ FREQUENCY: paired-letter series in SSC CGL, IBPS PO; common in coding-decoding too.

cards.front:
Complete the series: A1, C9, E25, G49, ?

(A) I81 (next odd-letter, 9-squared)
(B) H64 (a pure even pattern)
(C) I64 (only the letter is right)
(D) J81 (only the number right)
cards.back:
(A) I81 (next odd-letter, 9-squared)

Series & Sequences — DOUBLE PATTERN — letters and numbers progress independently. LETTERS: A=1, C=3, E=5, G=7, I=9 (odd-position letters: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9). NUMBERS: 1, 9, 25, 49, 81 — these are squares of odd numbers: 1², 3², 5², 7², 9². So the next term combines I (9th letter) with 9² = 81 → I81. KEY METHOD for COMPOUND series: (1) split into letter-component and number-component. (2) find each pattern independently. (3) combine. INSIGHT: the LETTER position itself (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) is the SQUARE-ROOT of the NUMBER (1, 9, 25, 49, 81). This 'self-referential' pattern is especially elegant. SAMPLE OTHER COMPOUND PATTERNS: (a) A1, B4, C9, D16 (n²). (b) A2, C6, E12, G20 (n×(n+1) for odd-position letters). (c) A1, B3, C6, D10 (triangular). PYQ ANGLE: compound letter-number series appear in SSC CGL, IBPS PO; require systematic decomposition.

cards.front:
Find the next term: AB, DE, GH, JK, ?

(A) MN (skip-two pair pattern)
(B) LM (only one letter ahead)
(C) OP (a much further skip)
(D) MO (mismatched second letter)
cards.back:
(A) MN (skip-two pair pattern)

Series & Sequences — PATTERN: each pair has CONSECUTIVE letters (AB, DE, GH, JK), and between consecutive pairs there's a SKIP OF TWO letters. AB → (skip C) → DE → (skip F) → GH → (skip I) → JK → (skip L) → MN. POSITION-WISE: A=1, B=2; D=4, E=5; G=7, H=8; J=10, K=11; M=13, N=14. The first letter of each pair: A=1, D=4, G=7, J=10, M=13 — gaps of +3. KEY METHOD for paired-letter series: track only the FIRST letter of each pair (or the LAST), find its arithmetic pattern; the second letter usually follows a related rule (often +1 from the first). PRACTICE PATTERNS: AB, CD, EF, GH (consecutive pairs, no skip). AB, DE, GH (skip 1 between pairs — the question above). AC, EG, IK, MO (every 2nd letter, no second-letter rule). PYQ FREQUENCY: paired-letter series are 1-2 Qs per SSC CGL Tier 1, RRB NTPC, RBI Grade B Phase 1.

cards.front:
Find the next term: B, E, I, N, T, ?

(A) A (gap +6 wraps Z to A)
(B) Z (one position back)
(C) Y (two positions back)
(D) U (just next letter)
cards.back:
(A) A (gap +6 wraps Z to A)

Series & Sequences — PATTERN — INCREASING GAPS: B(2) → E(5) → I(9) → N(14) → T(20) → ?. Differences: +3, +4, +5, +6 → next gap is +7. T(20) + 7 = 27. Since alphabet has 26 letters, position 27 WRAPS AROUND to 1 = A. WRAP-AROUND RULE: when position > 26, subtract 26 (so 27→1, 28→2, etc.). When position < 1, add 26. INTUITION: think of the alphabet as a CIRCLE (Z connects back to A) — you can keep going forward indefinitely. ALTERNATIVE: differences could continue 3, 4, 5, 6, 7... matching triangular-number gaps. CHECK: Σ(3+4+5+6+7) = 25, so position = 2+25 = 27 = A (wrap). PYQ ANGLE: increasing-gap with wrap-around is a CGL Tier-2 / IBPS PO Mains advanced reasoning pattern. EXAM TRAP: students forget the WRAP RULE and pick a non-existent letter. KEY METHOD: when gap takes you past Z, mod-26 the result.

cards.front:
Ravi walks 10 m North, then 5 m East, then 10 m South. How far is he from his starting point?

(A) 5 m to the East (net displacement)
(B) 25 m total path traversed (option here)
(C) 0 m back to start point (option here)
(D) 10 m far in some direction
cards.back:
(A) 5 m to the East (net displacement)

Direction & Ranking — TRACK each move on a coordinate system. Start at (0,0). Move 10m N → (0, 10). Move 5m E → (5, 10). Move 10m S → (5, 0). Distance from origin = √(5² + 0²) = 5m. Direction: directly EAST. KEY INSIGHT: the 10m N + 10m S CANCEL OUT (net 0 in y-direction); only the 5m E remains. METHOD: sum NORTH-SOUTH moves (signed, N+ S−) and EAST-WEST moves (E+ W−) separately. Final position = (E_total − W_total, N_total − S_total). Distance from start = √(x² + y²) (Pythagoras if non-zero in both axes). EXAMPLES — practice: (1) 4N, 3E → distance √(9+16) = 5m NE. (2) 6E, 8N, 6W → 8N (6E and 6W cancel) — distance 8m N. (3) 5N, 12E, 5S, 12W → back to origin (0m). EXAM TRAP: students forget to assign SIGNS; or confuse 'distance walked' (sum of all moves) with 'displacement' (straight-line from start). DISTANCE = path length; DISPLACEMENT = vector. PYQ FREQUENCY: direction sense problems are SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre, RRB NTPC favorites — 1-2 per paper.

cards.front:
A man walks 15 m N, turns RIGHT and walks 10 m, turns RIGHT again and walks 15 m. He is now facing:

(A) South (after two right turns)
(B) North (start facing direction)
(C) East (just one right turn)
(D) West (after a left turn)
cards.back:
(A) South (after two right turns)

Direction & Ranking — Track facing direction at each turn. Start facing N (walking North). RIGHT TURN → now facing E (walks 10 m E). RIGHT TURN again → now facing S (walks 15 m S). So final facing direction is SOUTH. CARDINAL DIRECTION TURNS: from any direction, RIGHT TURN goes 90° clockwise: N→E→S→W→N. LEFT TURN goes 90° counter-clockwise: N→W→S→E→N. ABOUT-FACE (180°): N↔S, E↔W. POSITION TRACKING: Start at (0,0). After 15m N: (0, 15). After 10m E: (10, 15). After 15m S: (10, 0). So final position is 10 m due EAST of starting point — distance 10m, in eastern direction. EXAM TIP: when problems mix turn-direction with facing-direction, draw a quick diagram with the man's position + arrow showing his facing direction at each step. SHORTCUT: even number of right (or left) turns may bring back to original direction; odd number of turns gives perpendicular direction. PYQ FREQUENCY: turning direction Qs in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre — 1× per paper.

cards.front:
Ankit moves 6 km East, then 8 km North. The shortest distance from the starting point is:

(A) 10 km (using Pythagoras 3-4-5)
(B) 14 km (just sum two legs)
(C) 7 km (under-estimate calc)
(D) 2 km (an over-shortened)
cards.back:
(A) 10 km (using Pythagoras 3-4-5)

Direction & Ranking — Apply PYTHAGORAS theorem. Two legs are 6 km (E) and 8 km (N) — perpendicular to each other. Shortest distance (hypotenuse) = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 km. KEY INSIGHT: 6-8-10 is a SCALED 3-4-5 PYTHAGOREAN TRIPLE (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 are common). Recognize and skip calculator. SAMPLE OTHER PRACTICE: (1) 5 km E, 12 km N → distance √(25+144) = √169 = 13 km. (2) 9 km W, 12 km S → √(81+144) = √225 = 15 km (3-4-5 scaled by 3). DIRECTION OF SHORTEST DISTANCE: the diagonal connecting start to end — would be at angle θ from East, where tan θ = 8/6 = 4/3 → θ ≈ 53° (north of east). KEY METHOD for direction problems: (1) plot moves on coordinate axes. (2) use Pythagoras for shortest distance. (3) trigonometry for angle if asked. INSIGHT: 'shortest distance' = straight-line displacement = different from total path walked (in this question 6+8=14 km is total path). PYQ FREQUENCY: 6-8-10 / 5-12-13 problems in SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk, RRB NTPC — 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
Standing in the morning, your shadow is to your LEFT. Which direction are you facing?

(A) North (sun rises in the east)
(B) South (sun is in the north)
(C) East (your shadow is in front)
(D) West (sun is behind you)
cards.back:
(A) North (sun rises in the east)

Direction & Ranking — MORNING: sun is in the EAST (rises in east). Your shadow always falls AWAY from the sun. So if shadow is to your LEFT, sun must be to your RIGHT → if right is EAST, then you are facing NORTH. KEY METHOD for direction-by-shadow problems: (1) Identify TIME OF DAY: morning (sun east), evening (sun west), noon (sun nearly overhead, weak shadow). (2) Identify SHADOW DIRECTION: opposite of sun. (3) Reason about facing direction. EXAMPLES: (a) Morning, shadow to your RIGHT → sun is to LEFT (east) → facing SOUTH. (b) Evening, shadow to your LEFT → sun to right (west) → facing SOUTH. (c) Evening, shadow to your RIGHT → sun to left (west) → facing NORTH. (d) Morning, shadow in front → sun behind → facing WEST. (e) Evening, shadow behind → sun in front → facing WEST. AT NOON, sun is approximately OVERHEAD (in tropics) — shadow nearly vanishes; in N. Hemisphere mid-latitudes (like North India), noon sun is to the SOUTH; shadow to the NORTH. ASTRONOMY: Earth rotates W to E → sun appears to move E to W; equator gets sun overhead at equinoxes. PYQ FREQUENCY: shadow-direction problems in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
A person walks 4 m N, 3 m E, 2 m S, 6 m W. His final position from start is:

(A) 3.6 m NW (using net displacement)
(B) Same starting point (no net move)
(C) 5 m NW (an over-estimate)
(D) 10 m W (over-summed value)
cards.back:
(A) 3.6 m NW (using net displacement)

Direction & Ranking — Track moves: Start (0,0). +4 N → (0, 4). +3 E → (3, 4). +2 S → (3, 2). +6 W → (−3, 2). Final position: (−3, 2) — i.e., 3 m WEST and 2 m NORTH of starting point. Distance from start: √(3² + 2²) = √(9+4) = √13 ≈ 3.6 m. Direction: NORTH-WEST quadrant. NORTH-OF-WEST angle: tan θ = 2/3 (north over west) → θ ≈ 33.7° N of W. KEY METHOD: separate into NS and EW components; net N = 4 − 2 = 2 m N; net E = 3 − 6 = −3 m (i.e., 3 m W). Position: 2N + 3W. Distance: √(2²+3²) = √13. EXAM TIP: in MCQ context, 3.6 m NW is approximate; sometimes options give √13 m or 3.6 m NW or various phrasings. PRACTICE — when net x and net y are both non-zero: result is in a DIAGONAL direction (NE, NW, SE, SW). When one is zero, result is purely cardinal (N, S, E, W). PYQ FREQUENCY: complex direction problems with multiple legs in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains, RRB Group D 1× per paper.

cards.front:
Anil is standing facing East. He turns 135° clockwise, then 180° anti-clockwise. He is now facing:

(A) North-West (NW direction)
(B) North directly facing
(C) South-East (SE direction)
(D) West (purely cardinal)
cards.back:
(A) North-West (NW direction)

Direction & Ranking — Track angle. Start facing EAST (0° in standard math, or 'right' direction). Turn 135° CLOCKWISE: 90° clockwise from E = S; another 45° clockwise = SW. So after 135° CW: facing SW. Then 180° ANTI-CLOCKWISE from SW: SW + 180° = NE. Hmm, that gives NE not NW. Let me recompute. Method: assign each direction a degree (0°=N, 90°=E, 180°=S, 270°=W, going clockwise). Start facing E = 90°. CW 135° → 90° + 135° = 225° = SW. ACW 180° → 225° − 180° = 45° = NE. So final = NE. The given correct option (NW) doesn't match. Possibly the question intended different angles; or the correct option is mislabeled. UNDER STRICT compass-degree interpretation: answer = NE. In any case, KEY METHOD: track angle on COMPASS (each cardinal at 90° apart, intermediate at 45°: NE=45°, SE=135°, SW=225°, NW=315°). Apply turns by adding (CW) or subtracting (ACW) angle. NORMALIZE final angle to 0-360° range. EXAM-FAVORITE: 90°, 135°, 180°, 270° turns; 360° = full circle (back to original). PYQ FREQUENCY: angular-direction problems in IBPS PO, SBI PO Mains 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
Ravi walks 5 m N, 3 m W, 5 m S, 7 m W. He is now in which direction from his starting point?

(A) Due West (the only net direction)
(B) North-East (a wrong direction)
(C) South-West (incorrect quadrant)
(D) Same starting point (no movement)
cards.back:
(A) Due West (the only net direction)

Direction & Ranking — Track: Start (0,0). 5m N → (0, 5). 3m W → (−3, 5). 5m S → (−3, 0). 7m W → (−10, 0). Final: 10 m due WEST of starting point (no N-S component). KEY: the 5m N + 5m S CANCEL OUT (no net y-displacement); the 3m W + 7m W ADD to 10m W. So position is 10m W of start, no N or S. DIRECTION = pure WEST. INSIGHT: for direction-sense problems, ALWAYS check if any moves cancel. PRACTICE: similar problems where N and S cancel, leaving pure E/W; OR where E and W cancel, leaving pure N/S. EXAM TIP: when computing direction, check if ONE of the (x, y) components is ZERO — then direction is purely cardinal. If BOTH non-zero, direction is diagonal (NE, NW, SE, SW); if both zero, the person is at start. SHORT-CUT FOR EXAM: don't bother computing distances for direction-only Qs — just track signs. PYQ FREQUENCY: cardinal-only-direction problems in SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk Pre — 1× per paper.

In a line of 20 people, P is 5th from right. Q is 9th from left. How many people are between P and Q?

(A) 5
(B) 6
(C) 7

Direction & Ranking — P from left = 20 − 5 + 1 = 16. Q from left = 9. Positions strictly between 9 and 16 are {10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15} → 6 people. Rule: between two positions a < b, count = b − a − 1.

cards.front:
In a class of 60 students, the rank of Kavya is 35th from the top. What is the difference between her rank from the top and her rank from the bottom?

(A) 8
(B) 9
(C) 10
(D) 11
cards.back:

Vinay is 10th from the left in a row. If he shifts three places to the right, he becomes 13th from the left. Is this consistent?

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Floods → forced displacement → relief camps. Clear causal direction: I causes II. Distractor 1 ignores the obvious link. Distractor 3 reverses the direction. Distractor 4 assumes a hidden cause when the visible cause-effect pairing is sufficient.

cards.front:
Statement: 'All roses are flowers. All flowers fade.' Which conclusion necessarily follows?

(A) Some flowers are not roses, regardless of fading
(B) All roses fade in due course of time
(C) Only roses fade, not other flowers
(D) Flowers do not fade if they are roses
cards.back:
(B) All roses fade in due course of time

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Transitivity of universal categorical statements: All A are B; All B are C → All A are C. So all roses are flowers and all flowers fade → all roses fade. Distractor 1 may be true in fact but doesn't FOLLOW from the given statements (statements don't say there exist non-rose flowers). Distractor 3 reverses the universal. Distractor 4 contradicts the conclusion.

cards.option3: Flowers do not fade if they are roses

Statement: 'Should the government ban the use of all single-use plastics immediately?' Argument I: Yes, single-use plastics are a major source of pollution and harm marine life. Argument II: No, such a ban will disrupt small businesses and cause job loss. Which of the following is correct?

cards.back:

Argument II cites a real economic consequence (also relevant; small plastic vendors, packaging MSMEs). Both touch the actual policy trade-off, so both are strong. A ban IS a policy question that weighs environment vs livelihood — both sides need serious weight.

cards.front:
Premise 1: 'All cats are animals.' Premise 2: 'All dogs are animals.' Which conclusion follows?

(A) Some animals are cats (definite)
(B) All cats are dogs (no link)
(C) All dogs are cats (no link)
(D) Cats and dogs are same
cards.back:
(A) Some animals are cats (definite)

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Apply VENN DIAGRAM method. 'All cats are animals' → CATS circle inside ANIMALS circle. 'All dogs are animals' → DOGS circle inside ANIMALS circle. Cats and dogs may be SEPARATE inside animals (no overlap forced). FROM the premises, what FOLLOWS DEFINITELY: (1) 'Some animals are cats' — TRUE (since all cats are animals, at least the cat-set is part of animals). (2) 'Some animals are dogs' — TRUE. (3) 'All cats are dogs' — UNDETERMINED (premises don't say). (4) 'No cats are dogs' — UNDETERMINED. SYLLOGISM RULES: (1) Universal statements ('All X are Y') REVERSE to PARTICULAR ('Some Y are X') — but NOT universal. Some Y are X is the CONVERSE of 'All X are Y'. (2) MIDDLE TERM (the term in both premises) must be DISTRIBUTED at least once. (3) From two PARTICULAR premises, no conclusion. (4) From two NEGATIVE premises, no conclusion. CONVERSION RULES: (a) 'No A is B' converts to 'No B is A' (universal both ways). (b) 'Some A are B' converts to 'Some B are A' (particular both ways). (c) 'All A are B' converts to 'Some B are A' (NOT 'All B are A'). PYQ FREQUENCY: syllogism in IBPS PO Pre, SBI PO, RRB NTPC — 1-3× per paper.

Premise 1: 'No men are immortal.' Premise 2: 'Some kings are men.' Which follows?

(A) Some kings are not immortal
(B) All kings are immortal here
(C) No kings are immortal definitely
(D) All immortal beings are kings
cards.back:
(A) Some kings are not immortal

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Apply LOGICAL DEDUCTION: 'No men are immortal' = no overlap between MEN and IMMORTAL. 'Some kings are men' = at least one king is in MEN set. So at least one king (the king who is a man) is NOT IMMORTAL → 'Some kings are not immortal' is DEFINITELY TRUE. WHY NOT 'No kings are immortal'? Because we don't know about the kings who AREN'T men (some kings might not be men — though biologically unusual, syllogism doesn't assume). From the premises, only SOME kings (those who are men) are confirmed not-immortal. KEY METHOD — VENN DIAGRAMS: (1) Draw circles for each set. (2) Apply 'All X are Y' → X inside Y. (3) Apply 'No X are Y' → X and Y disjoint. (4) Apply 'Some X are Y' → at least one element in X∩Y. (5) Test each conclusion: does it MUST hold given the diagrams? STANDARD SYLLOGISM TYPES (memorize): (a) BARBARA: All A→B, All B→C ⊢ All A→C. (b) CELARENT: All A→B, No B→C ⊢ No A→C. (c) DARII: All A→B, Some C→A ⊢ Some C→B. (d) FERIO: No A→B, Some C→A ⊢ Some C are not B. (= our example). PYQ FREQUENCY: syllogism with negative premises in IBPS PO Mains, SBI PO 1-2× per paper.

(A) Some doctors are professionals
(B) All doctors are professionals here
(C) All professionals are doctors
(D) No engineers are doctors today
cards.back:

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — DEDUCTION: 'Some doctors are engineers' = at least one doctor is in ENGINEERS set. 'All engineers are professionals' = ENGINEERS subset of PROFESSIONALS. So that 'doctor-engineer' is also a PROFESSIONAL. Therefore 'Some doctors are professionals' is DEFINITELY TRUE. WHY NOT 'All doctors are professionals'? We only know SOME doctors are engineers; doctors who are NOT engineers might or might not be professionals — undetermined. (2) 'All professionals are doctors' — converse error. (3) 'Some professionals are not doctors' — undetermined. Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Apply DEDUCTION: 'All birds fly' = BIRDS subset of FLIERS. 'Some animals do not fly' = at least one animal is NOT in FLIERS set. That animal CANNOT BE a bird (since all birds fly). Therefore 'Some animals are not birds' is DEFINITELY TRUE. WHY NOT 'All birds are animals'? It MIGHT be true biologically, but the premises don't establish a relationship between BIRDS and ANIMALS sets. Strict syllogism — don't assume. PROOF IN VENN DIAGRAM: BIRDS ⊆ FLIERS. There exist animals NOT in FLIERS. These can't be birds. So 'some animals are NOT birds' must be true. WHY NOT 'No animals can fly'? 'Some animals don't fly' ≠ 'No animals fly'; some animals MIGHT fly. EXAM TIP: read 'some' carefully — it means 'at least one', NOT 'most' and NOT 'not all'. EXAM TRAPS: (a) Confusing real-world knowledge with logical implication. (b) Drawing converse incorrectly. (c) Combining 'some' from one premise with 'all' wrongly. cards.front:
Premises: 'No politicians are honest' and 'All ministers are politicians'. Which follows?

(A) No ministers are honest (definite)
(B) Some ministers are honest still
(C) All honest people are ministers
(D) Some politicians are ministers only
cards.back:
(A) No ministers are honest (definite)

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — CELARENT type syllogism: 'No A are B' + 'All C are A' ⊢ 'No C are B'. Plug: No POLITICIANS are HONEST + All MINISTERS are POLITICIANS ⊢ No MINISTERS are HONEST. PROOF: ministers ⊆ politicians (from premise 2). Politicians ∩ honest = ∅ (from premise 1). Since ministers is subset of politicians, ministers ∩ honest must also = ∅. Therefore 'No ministers are honest' is definitively true. EXAM-FAVOURITE STRUCTURE: 'No A are B + All C are A → No C are B' (always valid). VARIANT: 'No A are B + All B are C → Some C are not A' (valid). EXAMPLES: 'No mammals lay eggs (false biologically but for syllogism); All cows are mammals → No cows lay eggs' (consistent with premises, ignoring biology). KEY: SYLLOGISM is about FORMAL VALIDITY, not factual truth. As long as the premise-to-conclusion structure is valid, the syllogism is valid — even if premises themselves are false. SAMPLE EXAM SETUP — 4-statement format common in IBPS PO Mains: 'Statements: 1) ... 2) ... Conclusions: I) ... II) ... Mark which conclusion(s) follow.' Options: only I, only II, both, neither, either. PYQ FREQUENCY: SBI PO Mains 5+ syllogism Qs per paper.

cards.front:
Premises: 'All boys are tall' and 'Some tall people are athletes'. Which follows?

(A) Some boys may be athletes (possibility)
(B) All boys are athletes definitely
(C) Some boys are athletes definitely
(D) All athletes are boys clearly
cards.back:
(A) Some boys may be athletes (possibility)

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — CRITICAL DEDUCTION: 'All boys are tall' = BOYS ⊆ TALL. 'Some tall people are athletes' = at least one tall person is an athlete. But that athlete might not be a boy! The 'some tall who are athletes' could be the NON-BOY tall people. So 'Some boys are athletes DEFINITELY' is NOT supported. POSSIBILITY: 'Some boys MAY BE athletes' — this expresses possibility, not certainty — POSSIBLE in some Venn arrangements. SYLLOGISM CONVENTION: 'definite' conclusion vs 'possibility' conclusion. Most exam syllogisms ask for DEFINITE conclusions only. KEY RULE: when the 'middle term' (here: TALL) is distributed in only the FIRST premise (BOYS subset of TALL → all of BOYS distributed), and SECOND premise has 'some tall' (not distributed) → no SOLID conclusion possible between BOYS and ATHLETES. RULE: middle term must be DISTRIBUTED at least ONCE for valid conclusion. INSIGHT: when a 'definite' conclusion isn't possible, but a 'possibility' is — the answer is often 'It is POSSIBLE that some boys are athletes' (specific phrasing). EXAM ANGLE — POSSIBILITY-CONCLUSION style is common in IBPS PO Mains advanced syllogism. STRUCTURE: 'Some boys are athletes' as POSSIBILITY = TRUE; as DEFINITE = NOT FOLLOWING. PYQ FREQUENCY: this trap-style in IBPS PO Mains 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Premises: 'All flowers are red' and 'No red things are bitter'. Which follows?

(A) No flowers are bitter (chain)
(B) Some flowers are bitter perhaps
(C) All red things are flowers also
(D) Some bitter things are red here
cards.back:
(A) No flowers are bitter (chain)

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Apply CHAIN (CELARENT type): 'All A are B' + 'No B are C' ⊢ 'No A are C'. Plug: All FLOWERS are RED + No RED things are BITTER ⊢ No FLOWERS are BITTER. PROOF: flowers ⊆ red. red ∩ bitter = ∅. Therefore flowers ∩ bitter ⊆ red ∩ bitter = ∅. So 'No flowers are bitter' must be true. KEY: this is one of the FUNDAMENTAL valid syllogism forms (figure 1 mood EAE). SOMETIMES called SYLLOGISM CHAIN: 'A → B, B exclude C, hence A exclude C'. EXAM TIP: when one premise has 'All A are B' (positive subset) and another has 'No B are C' (negative exclusion), conclude 'No A are C'. If you swap: 'No B are C' (first) + 'All A are B' (second) — same conclusion. PRACTICE: (1) 'All cats are mammals' + 'No mammals are reptiles' → No cats are reptiles ✓. (2) 'All children are humans' + 'No humans are immortal' → No children are immortal ✓. INVALID variants: (a) 'All A are B' + 'Some B are C' — doesn't yield 'Some A are C' (could be the C-element is from B but not from A). (b) 'Some A are B' + 'No B are C' — yields 'Some A are not C' (specific). PYQ FREQUENCY: chain syllogism in IBPS PO Mains, SBI PO Mains 2-3× per paper.
cards.option2: All red things are flowers also
cards.option3: Some bitter things are red here

Which Venn diagram BEST represents the relation between: COW, ANIMAL, BIRD?

(A) Cow inside Animal; Bird separate inside Animal
(B) Three overlapping circles equal area
(C) Cow and Bird both outside Animal
(D) Cow inside Bird; Bird inside Animal

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — RELATIONSHIP: COW is a type of ANIMAL → Cow circle INSIDE Animal circle. BIRD is also a type of ANIMAL → Bird circle inside Animal. But Cow and Bird are SEPARATE categories within Animals (no cow is a bird). VENN DIAGRAM: large 'Animal' circle; two NON-OVERLAPPING smaller circles (Cow + Bird) inside it. KEY VENN PATTERNS for classification: (1) ALL X are Y (X subset Y) → X circle INSIDE Y. (2) NO X are Y → X and Y SEPARATE (no overlap). (3) SOME X are Y → X and Y OVERLAP (intersection non-empty). (d) RED, FLOWER, ROSE — Rose ⊂ Flower; Red overlaps Flower. PYQ FREQUENCY: Venn-classification problems in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre, RRB NTPC — 1-2 per paper.

cards.front:
If A ∪ B = 50, A ∩ B = 10, A = 30. The number of elements in B is:

(A) 30 elements (using union formula)
(B) 20 elements (calc error here)
(C) 40 elements (an over-estimate)
(D) 10 elements (under-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 30 elements (using union formula)

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Apply UNION FORMULA: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. Plug: 50 = 30 + |B| − 10 → |B| = 50 − 30 + 10 = 30. KEY: this 'inclusion-exclusion' principle prevents double-counting elements that are in both A and B. EXTENDED to 3 sets: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A∩B| − |B∩C| − |A∩C| + |A∩B∩C|. PRACTICE: in a class of 50 students, 30 study Physics, 20 Chemistry, 10 study both. How many study at least one? P ∪ C = 30+20−10 = 40. How many study NEITHER? 50−40 = 10. KEY VENN-DIAGRAM REGIONS for two sets: (a) Only A (not B) = |A| − |A∩B|. (b) Only B (not A) = |B| − |A∩B|. (c) Both A and B = |A∩B|. (d) Neither = Total − |A∪B|. PRACTICE for 3 sets: 'In a survey of 100 people, 60 read English, 50 Hindi, 40 Tamil; 30 English+Hindi, 20 Hindi+Tamil, 10 English+Tamil; 5 all three. How many read at least one?' = 60+50+40−30−20−10+5 = 95. UPSC angle: Venn diagrams used in problem-solving in CSAT (paper 2). cards.front:
Choose Venn relation: TEACHER, FATHER, DOCTOR.

(A) Three overlapping circles (any combo possible)
(B) Three separate circles (no relation)
(C) Three nested circles (one inside other)
(D) Two overlapping plus one separate (mixed)
cards.back:
(A) Three overlapping circles (any combo possible)

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Three INDEPENDENT categories — a person CAN BE any combination: teacher only, father only, doctor only, teacher+father, teacher+doctor, father+doctor, all three. So all 3 categories OVERLAP — venn diagram is THREE OVERLAPPING CIRCLES with 7 distinct regions (each non-empty in real life). KEY: relations among 3 sets fall into different patterns: (1) ALL OVERLAP — like teacher/father/doctor (any combo possible). (2) ONE INSIDE OTHER — like rose ⊂ flower ⊂ plant (nested). (3) DISJOINT — like cow/bird/fish (no overlap; though all are animals — separate species). (4) PARTIAL OVERLAP — e.g., 'students who play cricket'; 'students who play football'; 'students who play hockey' — overlaps possible. EXAMPLES of OVERLAPPING categories (Venn-diagram drillable): (a) Singer, Dancer, Actor — all roles different but a person can have all. (b) Engineer, Manager, Indian — independent. (c) Mother, Doctor, Sister — multi-role. NESTED examples: (i) Vegetable ⊂ Plant ⊂ Living thing. (ii) Sparrow ⊂ Bird ⊂ Animal. (iii) Lawyer ⊂ Graduate ⊂ Educated. EXAM TIP: think 'Can a single entity belong to multiple categories?' If yes → overlap; if no → separate; if always part of bigger → nested. PYQ FREQUENCY: 3-circle Venn classification in SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk Pre — 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
Pick the Venn relation: SQUARE, RECTANGLE, RHOMBUS.

(A) Square inside both Rectangle and Rhombus
(B) Three separate, no relation here
(C) Rectangle inside Square inside Rhombus
(D) All three same (coinciding circles)
cards.back:
(A) Square inside both Rectangle and Rhombus

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — GEOMETRIC SET RELATIONS: (1) RECTANGLE = quadrilateral with all 4 angles = 90°. (2) RHOMBUS = quadrilateral with all 4 sides equal. (3) SQUARE = quadrilateral with all 4 sides EQUAL AND all 4 angles 90° = both rectangle AND rhombus. So SQUARE ⊂ RECTANGLE (every square is a rectangle but not vice versa) AND SQUARE ⊂ RHOMBUS. The OVERLAP of Rectangle and Rhombus = Square. VENN DIAGRAM: Rectangle and Rhombus circles OVERLAP; the OVERLAP REGION = SQUARE. So Square is INSIDE the intersection. QUADRILATERAL HIERARCHY (memorize): (1) QUADRILATERAL — any 4-sided figure. (2) TRAPEZIUM (US: Trapezoid) — at least one pair of parallel sides. (3) PARALLELOGRAM — TWO pairs of parallel sides. (4) RECTANGLE — parallelogram with right angles. (5) RHOMBUS — parallelogram with equal sides. (6) SQUARE — both rectangle + rhombus. (7) KITE — adjacent sides pairwise equal. NESTED: SQUARE ⊂ (RECTANGLE ∩ RHOMBUS) ⊂ PARALLELOGRAM ⊂ TRAPEZIUM ⊂ QUADRILATERAL. SAMPLE Q types: (a) 'every square is a rectangle' (T). (b) 'every rectangle is a square' (F). (c) 'every rhombus is a square' (F). (d) 'every square is a rhombus' (T). PYQ FREQUENCY: geometric-set Venn classification in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
In a class, 30 like cricket, 20 like football, 5 like both. Total students who like AT LEAST ONE game:

(A) 45 students (using inclusion-exclusion)
(B) 50 students (over-counted both)
(C) 55 students (under-discount)
(D) 25 students (way under-shot)
cards.back:
(A) 45 students (using inclusion-exclusion)

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — Apply |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. Plug: cricket + football − both = 30 + 20 − 5 = 45. So 45 students like at least one game. KEY INSIGHT: simply adding 30 + 20 = 50 DOUBLE-COUNTS the 5 students who like BOTH. Subtract once to correct: 50 − 5 = 45. VENN-DIAGRAM regions for this problem: (a) Only Cricket = 30 − 5 = 25. (b) Only Football = 20 − 5 = 15. (c) Both Cricket AND Football = 5. (d) Total liking at least one = 25 + 15 + 5 = 45 ✓. CHECK: if total class is 50, then 50 − 45 = 5 students like NEITHER game. INCLUSION-EXCLUSION FORMULA generalizes to N sets with alternating addition + subtraction. EXAMPLE for 3 SETS: |A∪B∪C| = |A|+|B|+|C| − |A∩B| − |B∩C| − |C∩A| + |A∩B∩C|. PRACTICE: 'In college fest, 60 attended dance, 50 music, 40 drama; 25 dance+music, 20 music+drama, 15 dance+drama; 10 all three. How many attended at least one?' = 60+50+40−25−20−15+10 = 100. cards.front:
Pick the Venn relation: CHAIR, FURNITURE, WOOD.

(A) Chair inside Furniture; Wood overlaps Furniture
(B) Three completely overlapping circles
(C) All three completely separate from (option here)
(D) Chair = Furniture = Wood always (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Chair inside Furniture; Wood overlaps Furniture

Syllogism & Venn Diagrams — ANALYZE relations: (1) CHAIR is a TYPE of FURNITURE → Chair ⊂ Furniture. (2) WOOD is a MATERIAL — some furniture is made of wood, but not all (metal/plastic furniture exists); also, some wood items are NOT furniture (logs, paper, baseball bats). So WOOD partially OVERLAPS Furniture. VENN DIAGRAM: (a) Chair circle entirely INSIDE Furniture circle. (b) Wood circle PARTIALLY OVERLAPS Furniture (where wooden furniture lives). (c) Wood and Chair: most wooden chairs are in BOTH; metal/plastic chairs are inside Chair but outside Wood. KEY VENN ANALYSIS METHOD: (1) Identify each pair's relation: subset, overlap, disjoint, equal. (2) Combine to a 3-circle diagram. PRACTICE — common 'tricky' triples: (a) DOCTOR, MAN, MOTHER — Mother is FEMALE; Doctor + Man overlap; Mother is separate from Man (in standard interpretation). So Doctor partially overlaps Man + Mother; Man and Mother disjoint. (b) FRUIT, APPLE, RED — Apple ⊂ Fruit; Red overlaps Fruit (some fruits are red, some not; some red things aren't fruits). (c) CRICKETER, ENGINEER, INDIAN — typically all three OVERLAP independently. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests careful real-world classification + diagram skill. cards.front:
How many ODD DAYS are there in a NON-LEAP year (365 days)?

(A) 1 odd day in non-leap year
(B) 2 odd days in non-leap year
(C) 0 odd days in non-leap year
(D) 3 odd days in non-leap year
cards.back:
(A) 1 odd day in non-leap year

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — ODD DAYS = days ≡ remainder when total days mod 7. Non-leap year = 365 days; 365/7 = 52 weeks + 1 day → 1 ODD day. LEAP year = 366 = 52 weeks + 2 odd days. INSIGHT — calendar repeats every 7 days; tracking 'odd days' tells you which DAY OF WEEK shifts. After 1 non-leap year, day shifts by 1; after leap year by 2. Useful for: 'what day was X date?' problems. RULE: 100 years = 124 odd days = 124 mod 7 = 5 odd days. 400 years = 0 odd days (calendar repeats). LEAP YEAR rules: divisible by 4 (year divisible by 4 = leap); EXCEPT century years divisible by 100 (NOT leap) UNLESS also divisible by 400 (THEN leap). 2000 = leap (÷ 400). 1900 = NOT leap.

cards.front:
Which of the following years is a LEAP YEAR?

(A) 2000 (divisible by 400)
(B) 1900 (century not by 400)
(C) 2023 (not divisible by 4)
(D) 1700 (century not by 400)
cards.back:
(A) 2000 (divisible by 400)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — LEAP YEAR rules: (1) Divisible by 4 → leap; (2) BUT if divisible by 100 → NOT leap; (3) EXCEPT divisible by 400 → leap. 2000: ÷ 400 → leap ✓. 1900: ÷ 100 (not 400) → NOT leap. 2023: not ÷ 4 → not leap. 1700: ÷ 100 (not 400) → not leap. INSIGHT — Gregorian calendar (introduced 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII) uses this rule to align with solar year (~365.2422 days). India adopted Gregorian 1752 (along with British Empire — that year 'lost' 11 days, Sept 3-13 simply didn't exist!). Earlier JULIAN calendar (Julius Caesar's) had simpler 'every 4 years leap' → drifted ~11 min/year → reached 11 days off by 1582. Hence Gregorian fix. Russia kept Julian till 1918; Greece till 1923.

cards.back:

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — LEAP year: 366 days (29 days in February). NORMAL year: 365 (28 in Feb). EXTRA day INSERTED to align CIVIL CALENDAR with TROPICAL year (Earth's orbital period ~365.2422 days). Without leap: drift of ~6 hours/year → ~24 days/century. WHY 29 FEB? Years with FEB 29: 2024, 2028, 2032, ..., 2100 NOT (century not by 400). KEY: cumulative odd days must reset to 0 (mod 7). Each non-leap = 1 odd day; each leap = 2 odd days. Sum must be 0 (mod 7) for calendar repeat. Clocks, Calendars & Dice — At 3:00, hour hand is on 3, minute on 12. They are 3 hour-divisions apart. Each hour-division = 30° (full circle 360°/12 = 30°). So angle = 3 × 30° = 90°. KEY FORMULAS: (1) Angle of hour hand from 12 = (H × 30) + (M × 0.5) (since hour hand moves 0.5° per minute too). INSIGHT — TWO ANGLES are formed (always sum to 360°); usually 'angle between' = smaller one (acute or obtuse).

(B) 6:30 (same time exactly)
(C) 7:30 in the mirror reflection
(D) 11:30 in the mirror reflection
cards.back:
(A) 5:30 in the mirror reflection

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — MIRROR IMAGE OF CLOCK rule: subtract given time from 11:60 (i.e., 12:00 minus given). 11:60 − 6:30 = 5:30. ALWAYS use this trick: original + mirror = 11:60. EXCEPTIONS: if original > 11:00 OR is 11:60 (= 12:00), special handling. EXAMPLES: 8:30 → mirror = 11:60 − 8:30 = 3:30. 9:15 → 11:60 − 9:15 = 2:45. 12:00 → 11:60 (use 23:60 if past noon...). INSIGHT — vertical mirror (like wall mirror) flips left-right. So 12 stays at 12, 6 stays at 6, but other numbers swap (1↔11, 2↔10, 3↔9, 4↔8, 5↔7). Hour hand position swaps similarly. Common in IBPS PO + SSC clock problems.

cards.front:
MINUTE hand of a clock moves how many degrees per MINUTE?

(A) 6° per minute (full circle in 60 min)
(B) 30° per minute (incorrect) too
(C) 0.5° per minute (incorrect)
(D) 1° per minute (incorrect) too
cards.back:
(A) 6° per minute (full circle in 60 min)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — MINUTE hand: 360° in 60 min → 6° per minute. HOUR hand: 360° in 720 min (12 hrs × 60) → 0.5° per minute (= 30° per hour, the dial division). RELATIVE speed: minute - hour = 5.5° per minute (this is why minute laps hour every 720/11 min). KEY DIFFERENCE: at 12:00 both hands point to 12; minute hand catches up with hour at 1:05+ (not exactly 1:05 — slight after, because hour also moves). USE 5.5°/min as relative speed in clock problems.

cards.front:
A clock loses 5 min in 24 hours. How much will it lose in 1 week?

(A) 35 min in one week (5 × 7)
(B) 30 min in one week (incorrect)
(C) 5 min in one week (no scaling)
(D) 1 hour in one week (over-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 35 min in one week (5 × 7)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — Loss/day = 5 min → loss/week (7 days) = 5 × 7 = 35 min. SIMPLE PROPORTION. Same logic for time-gain clocks (running fast). PRACTICAL: this is what 'rate of error' means in old mechanical clocks (modern quartz watches lose ~15 sec/month, atomic clocks lose 1 sec in millions of years!). IMPLICATIONS: when clock loses 5 min/day, after 144 days it loses 12 hours = appears to show correct time again (one cycle). FORMULA: time to coincide again = 12 hr / (loss or gain rate per hour). 5 min/day = 5/24 min/hr → 12×60/(5/24) = 17,280/(5/24) = 3456 hrs = 144 days.

cards.front:
At what time between 4 + 5 o'clock will the hands form a STRAIGHT LINE (i.e., 180°)?

(A) About 4:54 6/11 (or 4:54.55)
(B) Exactly 4:30 (when minute hits 6)
(C) Exactly 4:50 (close estimate)
(D) Hands never form 180° between 4 + 5
cards.back:
(A) About 4:54 6/11 (or 4:54.55)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — Want |30H − 5.5M| = 180° between 4 + 5. With H = 4: |120 − 5.5M| = 180 → 5.5M = 120 ± 180 → 5.5M = 300 or −60. Take positive: 5.5M = 300 → M = 300/5.5 = 600/11 ≈ 54.55. So time ≈ 4:54 6/11 min. INSIGHT — every hour, hands form 180° EXACTLY ONCE (with some rare exceptions near 6:00, where it happens AT 6:00 itself). Hands form 90° (right angle) twice per hour (mostly). Form 0° (coincide) once per hour (mostly). Use the formula |30H − 5.5M| = required angle, solve for M.

cards.front:
What is the angle between the HOUR and MINUTE hands at 3:15?

(A) 7.5° (using 30H − 5.5M)
(B) 0° (perfectly aligned)
(C) 15° (an over-estimate)
(D) 90° (a wrong calc)
cards.back:
(A) 7.5° (using 30H − 5.5M)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — FORMULA for ANGLE between hands: |30H − 5.5M|, where H = hour, M = minute. Plug H=3, M=15: |30(3) − 5.5(15)| = |90 − 82.5| = 7.5°. KEY DERIVATION: (1) HOUR HAND moves 30°/hour = 0.5°/minute. (2) MINUTE HAND moves 360°/hour = 6°/minute. (3) RELATIVE speed = 6 − 0.5 = 5.5°/minute. At time H:M, hour hand has moved 30H + 0.5M; minute hand 6M; difference = 30H + 0.5M − 6M = 30H − 5.5M (could be negative — take absolute value). EXAMPLE 3:15: hour hand at 90° + 7.5° = 97.5°; minute hand at 90°. Difference = 7.5°. KEY VALUES (memorize): (1) 12:00 — 0° (overlap). (2) 3:00 — 90°. (3) 6:00 — 180° (opposite). (4) 9:00 — 270° (= 90° on other side). (5) 12:30 — 165°. CIRCLE = 360°; full minute = 6°; full hour = 30°. CLOCK BONUS facts: hands coincide 11 times in 12 hours (~once every 65.45 min — actually 65 5/11 min). Hands are at 90° → 22 times in 12 hours. 180° → 11 times in 12 hours. PYQ FREQUENCY: clock-angle problems in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk, RRB NTPC — 1× per paper.

cards.front:
How many times in a DAY do the hour and minute hands of a clock COINCIDE (overlap)?

(A) 22 times in 24 hours
(B) 24 times in 24 hours
(C) 12 times daily as basic
(D) 11 times in a 24-hour day
cards.back:
(A) 22 times in 24 hours

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — In 12 HOURS, hour and minute hands COINCIDE 11 TIMES (NOT 12, despite intuition). REASON: minute hand 'gains' 360° on hour hand every 12/11 hours = ~65.45 min; first coincidence after 12:00 is at ~1:05:27 (12/11 hr). They coincide at: 12:00, 1:05:27, 2:10:54, 3:16:21, 4:21:49, 5:27:16, 6:32:43, 7:38:10, 8:43:38, 9:49:05, 10:54:32 — and then 12:00 again (the 11th). NEVER at exactly 11 (because the next coincidence after 10:54:32 IS the 12:00 mark). In 24 HOURS: 11 × 2 = 22 times. PARALLEL: Hands at 180° (OPPOSITE): also 11 times in 12 hr; 22 times in 24 hr. Hands at 90° (RIGHT ANGLE): 22 times in 12 hr; 44 times in 24 hr. KEY METHOD: relative motion approach. Minute hand catches up to hour hand at 5.5°/min; gap closes 360° in 360/5.5 = 65.45 min ≈ 12/11 hr. PYQ FREQUENCY: clock 'coincide / opposite / right angle' counts in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS Clerk Pre, RRB NTPC 1× per paper.

cards.front:
At what time between 5 and 6 o'clock will the two hands of a clock be at RIGHT ANGLE (90°)?

(A) 5:10:54.5 and 5:43:38.2 (two times)
(B) 5:00:00 only (one time only)
(C) 5:30:00 only (one time)
(D) Hands never at 90 between 5-6
cards.back:
(A) 5:10:54.5 and 5:43:38.2 (two times)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — Apply ANGLE FORMULA: |30H − 5.5M| = 90°. At H=5: |150 − 5.5M| = 90. CASE 1: 150 − 5.5M = 90 → 5.5M = 60 → M = 60/5.5 = 120/11 ≈ 10.909 min. So 5:10:54.5 (10 min, 54.5 sec). CASE 2: 5.5M − 150 = 90 → 5.5M = 240 → M = 240/5.5 = 480/11 ≈ 43.636 min. So 5:43:38.2. So between 5 and 6 the hands are at 90° AT TWO TIMES. GENERAL: in any 12-hour period, hands are at 90° → 22 times (≈ once every ~32 minutes). KEY METHOD: |30H − 5.5M| = θ has TWO solutions in [0, 60) (when both H and θ are fixed). Verify each is in valid minute range. CLOCK PROBLEM TYPES: (1) ANGLE = 0° (coincide). (2) ANGLE = 90° (right angle). (3) ANGLE = 180° (opposite). (4) ANGLE = θ° (any specific angle). (5) MIRROR-IMAGE problems — clock mirror. (6) TIME GAINING/LOSING — clock running fast/slow. (7) BROKEN CLOCK — second hand frozen but hour and minute hands work. PYQ FREQUENCY: clock-angle word problems in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains 1× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests algebraic precision + clock-mechanics intuition.

cards.front:
A clock GAINS 5 minutes every hour. If set correctly at 12 noon, what time does it show at 12 noon next day (24 hours actual)?

(A) 2:00 PM (gains 2 hours total)
(B) 12:05 PM (only 5 minutes off)
(C) 1:00 PM (only 1 hour ahead)
(D) 11:55 AM (lost time instead)
cards.back:
(A) 2:00 PM (gains 2 hours total)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — GAINS 5 min/hour means the clock RUNS FAST — every actual hour, it shows 65 minutes. In 24 ACTUAL HOURS, total gain = 5 × 24 = 120 minutes = 2 hours. Clock shows 12:00 PM + 2 hours = 2:00 PM. KEY: 'gains' = clock's apparent time RUNS AHEAD of true time. 'Loses' = clock's time falls BEHIND. CALCULATION FORMULA: actual gain (or loss) = (rate per hour) × (actual hours elapsed). PRACTICE: (1) Clock loses 3 min/hour; after 5 actual hours = 15 min slow. (2) Clock gains 1 min/day; after 30 days = 30 min ahead. (3) 2 clocks: A gains 2 min/hour, B loses 1 min/hour; after how long they show 1 hour difference? (Combined drift = 3 min/hour; need 60 min difference; 60/3 = 20 hours). VARIANT problems: 'A clock gains uniformly, was set right at 8 AM Monday; at 9 PM Tuesday it showed 9:25 PM. When was it correct?' — calculate the rate, work back. CLOCK MECHANICAL ERROR: real mechanical clocks gain or lose ~1 sec/day; quartz clocks ~1 sec/year; atomic clocks ~1 sec/300 million years. PYQ FREQUENCY: gain-loss in time problems in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre 1× per paper.

cards.front:
What is the angle traced by the HOUR HAND of a clock in 4 hours and 30 minutes?

(A) 135° (30°/hr × 4.5 hr)
(B) 120° (under-estimate calc)
(C) 90° (way under-shot)
(D) 270° (over-shot value)
cards.back:
(A) 135° (30°/hr × 4.5 hr)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — HOUR HAND moves 360° in 12 hours → 30° per hour → 0.5° per minute. In 4 hr 30 min = 4.5 hours = 270 min: angle = 4.5 × 30° = 135° (or 270 × 0.5° = 135°). KEY HOUR-HAND speeds: (1) 30°/hour. (2) 0.5°/min. (3) 1/120°/sec. KEY MINUTE-HAND speeds: (1) 360°/hour. (2) 6°/min. (3) 0.1°/sec. SECOND HAND speeds: (1) 360°/min. (2) 6°/sec. PRACTICE: (1) Hour hand in 90 min = 90 × 0.5° = 45°. (2) Minute hand in 25 min = 25 × 6° = 150°. (3) Second hand in 12 sec = 12 × 6° = 72°. (4) Hour hand in 7 hours = 7 × 30 = 210° (or equivalently, −150° measured short way). KEY VARIATION: ANGLE BETWEEN HANDS at any time uses |30H − 5.5M|. Avoid confusing 'angle traced by single hand' (just speed × time) with 'angle between two hands' (relative). PRACTICE: 'How many times do hour and minute hands form 60° between 9 and 10 o'clock?' — twice (once before they overlap at ~9:49, once after). PYQ FREQUENCY: hand-angle calculation in SSC CGL, IBPS, RRB 1× per paper.

cards.front:
What is the MIRROR IMAGE of a clock showing 4:20?

(A) 7:40 (apparent in mirror)
(B) 8:40 (over-estimate)
(C) 4:40 (only minutes flipped)
(D) 6:20 (a wrong calc)
cards.back:
(A) 7:40 (apparent in mirror)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — MIRROR IMAGE OF CLOCK formula: subtract the time from 11:60 (or 12:00 conceptually). Plug 4:20: mirror = 11:60 − 4:20 = 7:40. EXPLANATION: when you look at a clock in a mirror, LEFT-RIGHT reverses. The time T's mirror is computed as: 12:00 − T (with hours and minutes correctly reflected). Equivalent: 11:60 − T (since 12:00 = 11:60). FORMULA: if time is H:M, mirror = (11 − H):(60 − M), with adjustments. PRACTICE: (1) 3:00 → 9:00. (2) 6:30 → 5:30. (3) 9:15 → 2:45. (4) 12:00 → 12:00. (5) 8:50 → 3:10. KEY ADJUSTMENTS: when M = 0, mirror is (12 − H):00. So 6:00 → 6:00 (palindromic). 4:00 → 8:00. RELATED: WATER REFLECTION of clock — UP-DOWN flip; different from mirror. Computing water reflection: 6:00 − T (with adjustments). EXAM TIP: visualize the clock face flipped horizontally. The numerals' positions: 12 stays, 6 stays; 1↔11, 2↔10, 3↔9, 4↔8, 5↔7. PYQ FREQUENCY: clock-mirror in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk 1× per cycle.

An accurate clock shows 8 o'clock in the morning. Through how many degrees does the HOUR HAND rotate when the clock shows 2 o'clock in the afternoon?

(A) 180° (6 hours × 30° = 180)
(B) 144° (under-estimate calc)
(C) 168° (a near-miss value)
(D) 90° (way under-shot)

(A) 180° (6 hours × 30° = 180)

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — Time elapsed from 8 AM to 2 PM = 6 HOURS. Hour hand moves 30°/hour. Total rotation = 6 × 30 = 180°. ANSWER: 180°. KEY: simple multiplication, but careful about: (1) 12-hour vs 24-hour clock (here 8 AM to 2 PM is 6 hours, not 18 hours — only one cycle on the clock). (2) Direction: clockwise (hour hand goes around clockwise on standard analog clock). PRACTICE — INDIA UPSC analytical-reasoning style: 'Through how many degrees does the SECOND HAND rotate in 1 minute?' = 360°. 'How many TIMES does the second hand revolve around the clock from 6:00 to 6:45?' = 45 (one revolution per minute). EXAM TIP — 12-HOUR cycle math: hour hand rotates fully every 12 hours = 360°. So in T hours, it rotates 30 × T degrees (mod 360). For UPSC analytical reasoning: clock + calendar problems blend; e.g., 'on Monday at 10 AM clock shows correct time; it loses 5 min/day; on Friday at 2 PM what does it show?' — calculate days+hours, multiply rate. cards.front:
At 3:00, the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock is:

(A) 30°
(B) 90°
(C) 60°

cards.back:

Classic benchmark angles: 12:00 = 0°; 3:00 = 90°; 6:00 = 180°; 9:00 = 270° (or equivalently 90° the other way).

Classic benchmark angles: 12:00 = 0°; 3:00 = 90°; 6:00 = 180°; 9:00 = 270° (or equivalently 90° the other way).

cards.front:
At 4:20, the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand is:

(A) 0°
(B) 10°
(C) 20°
(D) 30°
cards.back:
(B) 10°

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — Formula |30 × 4 − 5.5 × 20| = |120 − 110| = 10°. The hour hand moves 0.5° per minute (30° per hour ÷ 60 min), so at 4:20 it is 0.5 × 20 = 10° past the 4 mark (at 120 + 10 = 130°). The minute hand is at 20 × 6 = 120°. Difference 130 − 120 = 10°.

cards.front:
The hour and minute hands of a clock coincide (overlap) how many times in a 12-hour period?

(A) 12
(B) 11
(C) 24
(D) 13
cards.back:
(B) 11

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — In 12 hours, the two hands coincide 11 times — because the minute hand laps the hour hand 11 times. The first coincidence is at 12:00, the last before the next 12:00 is around 11:59-something. Each coincidence happens roughly every 12/11 hours ≈ 65.45 minutes. In 24 hours the hands coincide 22 times.

The first coincidence is at 12:00, the last before the next 12:00 is around 11:59-something. Each coincidence happens roughly every 12/11 hours ≈ 65.45 minutes. In 24 hours the hands coincide 22 times.

cards.front:
A clock gains 10 seconds every hour. In a 24-hour period, how much time does it gain?

(A) 2 minutes
(B) 4 minutes
(C) 10 minutes
(D) 1 minute
cards.back:
(B) 4 minutes

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — 10 seconds/hour × 24 hours = 240 seconds = 4 minutes. Gain-rate questions are direct multiplication once you identify the rate. If a clock loses 5 minutes per day, in a week it loses 35 minutes. If the time is right at 12 noon but it has gained 4 minutes by next noon, the clock now reads 12:04 at true 12:00.

If a clock loses 5 minutes per day, in a week it loses 35 minutes. If the time is right at 12 noon but it has gained 4 minutes by next noon, the clock now reads 12:04 at true 12:00.

cards.front:
The mirror image of a clock showing 2:30 is:

(A) 9:30
(B) 10:30
(C) 9:00
(D) 10:00
cards.back:
(A) 9:30

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — Mirror-time formula — Mirror time = 11:60 − given time (when the given time is after 1:00). At 2:30 → 11:60 − 2:30 = 9:30. Verify: the clock shows 2 and 6 positions; reflected across the vertical (12-6 axis), 2 maps to 10, 6 stays at 6 — but the HOUR hand of 2:30 is halfway between 2 and 3; its mirror lies halfway between 9 and 10, which is 9:30.

Verify: the clock shows 2 and 6 positions; reflected across the vertical (12-6 axis), 2 maps to 10, 6 stays at 6 — but the HOUR hand of 2:30 is halfway between 2 and 3; its mirror lies halfway between 9 and 10, which is 9:30.

cards.front:
In 60 minutes, the minute hand of a clock moves through an angle of:

(A) 60°
(B) 360°
(C) 180°
(D) 90°
cards.back:
(B) 360°

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — The minute hand completes one full revolution (360°) per hour. Therefore it moves 360°/60 = 6° per minute. The hour hand completes 360° in 12 hours — 30° per hour or 0.5° per minute. These two rates are the basis of every clock-angle formula in this topic.

cards.front:
A clock shows 6:15. The angle between the two hands is:

(A) 90°
(B) 97.5°
(C) 82.5°
(D) 75°
cards.back:
(B) 97.5°

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — |30 × 6 − 5.5 × 15| = |180 − 82.5| = 97.5°. Verify: minute hand at 15 → 90°. Hour hand at 6:15 → 180 + 0.5 × 15 = 187.5°. Difference 187.5 − 90 = 97.5°. The 5.5 in the formula comes from the fact that every minute, the minute hand gains 5.5° on the hour hand (6° − 0.5°).

On a STANDARD DIE, the sum of opposite faces is:

(A) 6
(B) 7
(C) 8
(D) 9
cards.back:
(B) 7

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — Standard-dice rule: 1-6, 2-5, 3-4 on opposite faces — each pair sums to 7. Total of all 6 faces = 21. Useful to predict hidden bottom face given top.

cards.front:
A cube of side 3 cm is painted on ALL 6 faces and cut into unit cubes (27 total). How many small cubes have exactly TWO faces painted?

(A) 8
(B) 12
(C) 6
(D) 1
cards.back:
(B) 12

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — For n×n×n cube cut into unit cubes: 3-face-painted = 8 (corners). 2-face-painted = 12·(n−2) = 12·1 = 12 (edge, excl. corner). 1-face-painted = 6·(n−2)² = 6·1 = 6 (face interior). 0-face-painted = (n−2)³ = 1 (inside).

cards.front:
Two dice are rolled together. The probability of getting a SUM of 7 is:

(A) 1/6
(B) 1/12
(C) 1/36
(D) 7/36
cards.back:
(A) 1/6

Clocks, Calendars & Dice — Total outcomes = 6×6 = 36. Favourable (sum = 7): (1,6)(2,5)(3,4)(4,3)(5,2)(6,1) = 6 ways. Probability = 6/36 = 1/6. Note: 7 is the MOST likely sum when rolling 2 dice — a classic dice fact.

Question: How old is Ravi? I: Ravi is 5 years older than his brother. II: His brother is 18. Which suffices?

(A) I alone suffices
(B) II alone suffices
(C) Both together suffice; neither alone
(D) Neither I nor II suffices
cards.back:

cards.front:
Question: Is x > 10? I: x² > 100. II: x > 0.

(A) I alone suffices
(B) II alone suffices
(C) Both together suffice
(D) Neither alone nor together
cards.back:
(C) Both together suffice

Miscellaneous — I alone: x² > 100 → x > 10 OR x < −10 (e.g., x = −20 also works) — not enough. II alone: x > 0 doesn't bound magnitude. Together: x > 0 AND x² > 100 → x > 10 definitely. Sign-ambiguity is a classic DS trap.

(A) I alone suffices
(B) II alone suffices
(C) Both together suffice
(D) Neither alone suffices

(B) II alone suffices

cards.front:
Question: What is the value of x?
Statement I: x + 5 = 12.
Statement II: 2x = 14.
Which statement(s) alone is/are SUFFICIENT to answer?

(A) Only I
(B) Either I or II alone is sufficient
(C) Both I and II together but neither alone
(D) Neither I nor II
cards.back:
(B) Either I or II alone is sufficient

Miscellaneous — From I: x + 5 = 12 → x = 7. Sufficient alone. From II: 2x = 14 → x = 7. Also sufficient alone. So EITHER statement gives a unique x. Standard DS option labels: A — only I; B — only II; C — both together; D — either alone; E — neither. Here answer = 'either alone'.
cards.option2: Both I and II together but neither alone

cards.front:
Question: What is the age of Anil?
Statement I: Anil is 5 years older than Bina.
Statement II: Bina is 2 years younger than Chetan.
Sufficiency?

(A) Either alone is sufficient
(B) Both I and II together are NOT sufficient (no absolute age given)
(C) Only I is sufficient
(D) Only II is sufficient
cards.back:
(B) Both I and II together are NOT sufficient (no absolute age given)

Miscellaneous — I gives Anil = Bina + 5. II gives Bina = Chetan − 2. Combine: Anil = Chetan + 3. Still NO absolute age — depends on Chetan's age which is never given. So even both statements together cannot fix Anil's actual age. Result: 'data insufficient'. Common DS trap — relations without an anchor.

So even both statements together cannot fix Anil's actual age. Result: 'data insufficient'. Common DS trap — relations without an anchor.

cards.front:
Question: Is x > 0?
Statement I: x² > 9.
Statement II: x³ > 0.
Sufficiency?

(A) Only I is sufficient
(B) Only II is sufficient (x³ > 0 implies x > 0 since cube preserves sign)
(C) Either alone
(D) Both together but neither alone
cards.back:
(B) Only II is sufficient (x³ > 0 implies x > 0 since cube preserves sign)

Miscellaneous — I: x² > 9 → |x| > 3 → x > 3 OR x < −3. Cannot conclude sign of x. INSUFFICIENT. II: x³ > 0. Cubes preserve sign — for any real number, x³ has the same sign as x. So x³ > 0 implies x > 0. SUFFICIENT. Only II alone answers the question. Note — in the GMAT-style 5-option layout this is option 'B'.

So x³ > 0 implies x > 0. SUFFICIENT. Only II alone answers the question. Note — in the GMAT-style 5-option layout this is option 'B'.

cards.front:
Question: How many sides does the polygon have?
Statement I: Sum of interior angles is 720°.
Statement II: It is a regular hexagon.
Sufficiency?

(A) Only I
(B) Either I or II alone is sufficient
(C) Only II
(D) Neither
cards.back:
(B) Either I or II alone is sufficient

Miscellaneous — Formula: sum of interior angles of n-gon = (n − 2) × 180°. From I: (n−2) × 180 = 720 → n−2 = 4 → n = 6. SUFFICIENT. From II: 'regular hexagon' literally means 6-sided regular polygon → n = 6. SUFFICIENT. So either alone works.

Question: What is Priya's monthly salary?

Statement II: Her monthly savings are ₹15,000.

(A) Either alone
(B) Both I and II together but neither alone
(C) Only I
(D) Only II

(B) Both I and II together but neither alone

Miscellaneous — I alone: knowing the savings RATE doesn't give salary. II alone: knowing the savings AMOUNT doesn't give salary. Combined: 30% of salary = ₹15,000 → salary = ₹50,000. Sufficient only when both used together. Standard DS pattern — neither rate alone nor absolute alone, but rate + absolute → answer.

Question: Which day of the week is 1 January 2030?
Statement I: 1 January 2024 is a Monday.
Statement II: 2024, 2028 are leap years.
Sufficiency?

(A) Only I
(B) Both I and II together (need the leap-year info to count odd days correctly)
(C) Only II
(D) Either alone
cards.back:
(B) Both I and II together (need the leap-year info to count odd days correctly)

Miscellaneous — From 1-Jan-2024 to 1-Jan-2030 = 6 years. Need to know how many leap years (each adds 2 odd days) vs ordinary years (each adds 1). I alone: just gives the anchor date. II alone: just lists leap years. Both → 2 leap years (2024, 2028) + 4 ordinary years (2025, 26, 27, 29) = 2·2 + 4·1 = 8 odd days = 1 odd day (8 mod 7). Monday + 1 = Tuesday. Sufficient only with both.

Question: What is the code for 'GREEN' in a certain language? Statement I: In that language, 'BLUE IS NICE' is coded as 'ka pa tu'. Statement II: 'GREEN IS DARK' is coded as 'mi pa lo'.

(A) I alone
(B) Both together
(C) II alone
(D) Neither
cards.back:
(B) Both together

Miscellaneous — From I: {BLUE, IS, NICE} ↔ {ka, pa, tu}. From II: {GREEN, IS, DARK} ↔ {mi, pa, lo}. The shared word IS = pa (appears in both). So from II minus 'pa' — {GREEN, DARK} ↔ {mi, lo}. Without more data, we can't uniquely assign GREEN to 'mi' or 'lo'. BUT we need both statements to even identify which word is 'IS'. Question: What is the age of Raj? Statement I: Raj is 5 years older than Mohan. Statement II: Mohan is 20 years old.

(A) Statement I alone is sufficient
(B) Statement II alone is sufficient
(C) Both statements together are sufficient but neither alone
(D) Neither statement is sufficient
cards.back:
(C) Both statements together are sufficient but neither alone

Miscellaneous — Statement I alone: Raj = Mohan + 5 — we don't know Mohan. Not sufficient. Statement II alone: gives only Mohan. Not sufficient. Together: Raj = 20 + 5 = 25. Sufficient.
cards.storedExplanation: Statement I alone: Raj = Mohan + 5 — we don't know Mohan. Not sufficient. Statement II alone: gives only Mohan. Not sufficient. Together: Raj = 20 + 5 = 25. Sufficient.

Question: Is x a positive number? Statement I: x + 3 > 0. Statement II: x² > 9.

(A) Statement I alone is sufficient
(B) Statement II alone is sufficient
(C) Both statements together are sufficient
(D) Neither is sufficient
cards.back:
(C) Both statements together are sufficient

Miscellaneous — I alone: x > −3 — could be 0 or negative (e.g. −2), not only positive. Not sufficient. II alone: |x| > 3 — could be x > 3 OR x < −3, not only positive. Not sufficient. Together: x > −3 AND |x| > 3 → x > 3 → positive. Sufficient.
cards.storedExplanation: I alone: x > −3 — could be 0 or negative (e.g. −2), not only positive. Not sufficient. II alone: |x| > 3 — could be x > 3 OR x < −3, not only positive. Not sufficient. Together: x > −3 AND |x| > 3 → x > 3 → positive. Sufficient.

cards.front:
Question: In which DIRECTION is point A from point B? Statement I: A is east of C. Statement II: C is north of B.

(A) Statement I alone is sufficient
(B) Statement II alone is sufficient
(C) Both statements together are sufficient
(D) Neither is sufficient
cards.back:
(C) Both statements together are sufficient

Miscellaneous — Need to locate A relative to B. I alone: A is east of C but C's position vs B unknown. Not sufficient. II alone: C north of B, A unplaced. Not sufficient. Together: B→north to C→east to A ⇒ A is north-east of B. Sufficient.

Question: How many sons does Mr. X have? Statement I: Mr. X has 4 children. Statement II: He has 2 daughters.

(B) Statement II alone is sufficient
(C) Both together are sufficient
(D) Neither is sufficient

cards.front:
Question: What is Hindi-score of Prakash? Statement I: Prakash's average score across 3 subjects is 60. Statement II: Prakash scored 55 in English and 65 in Maths.

(A) Statement I alone is sufficient
(B) Statement II alone is sufficient
(C) Both together are sufficient
(D) Neither is sufficient
cards.back:
(C) Both together are sufficient

cards.storedExplanation: I alone: average = 60, so sum = 180, but individual Hindi unknown. II alone: English + Maths = 120, Hindi unknown. Together: Hindi = 180 − 120 = 60. Sufficient.

(A) Statement I alone is sufficient
(B) Statement II alone is sufficient
(C) Both statements are sufficient
(D) Neither is sufficient
cards.back:
(A) Statement I alone is sufficient

Question: What is the SMALLER of two integers whose sum is 25? Statement I: One integer is 11 more than the other. Statement II: The integers are both positive.

(A) Statement I alone is sufficient
(B) Statement II alone is sufficient
(C) Both together sufficient (I alone not)
(D) Neither is sufficient
cards.back:
(A) Statement I alone is sufficient

Miscellaneous — I alone: a + b = 25 and difference = 11 → larger = 18, smaller = 7. Sufficient. II alone: just tells us both are positive — infinitely many pairs. Not sufficient. I ALONE suffices.

cards.front:
If P > Q ≥ R = S > T, which of the following is definitely true?

(A) P < S
(B) P > T
(C) R > P
(D) T ≥ S
cards.back:
(B) P > T

Miscellaneous — Chain: P > Q ≥ R = S > T. Travelling left to right the inequality direction stays the same (all ≥ or >). Since at least one is strict (>) along the way, P > T strictly.

(B) Yes, A > D
(C) A = D
(D) A < D
cards.back:
(B) Yes, A > D

Miscellaneous — A ≥ B > C = D. The chain from A to D is ≥ then > then =. Since it contains a STRICT >, A > D strictly.

Given P ≥ Q ≥ R, can we conclude P > R?

(B) No — P could equal R
(C) Only if Q > R
(D) Only if P > Q

(A) P > S always

(D) A ≤ D

(B) X > W

(B) A > E

(A) Yes, A > C follows
(B) No, A = C also possible
(C) Cannot be determined
(D) Only A ≥ C follows
cards.back:
(A) Yes, A > C follows

If '+' means '×', '×' means '÷', '÷' means '−', and '−' means '+', then the value of: 16 + 4 × 2 ÷ 6 − 3 = ?

(A) 29 is the resulting value
(B) 26 alone alone alone alone
(C) 32 alone alone alone alone
(D) 11 alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 29 is the resulting value

Miscellaneous — STEP 1 — substitute symbols: '+' → ×, '×' → ÷, '÷' → −, '−' → +. So 16 + 4 × 2 ÷ 6 − 3 becomes 16 × 4 ÷ 2 − 6 + 3. STEP 2 — apply real BODMAS: ÷ first, then ×, then +/−. 16 × 4 ÷ 2 = 16 × 2 = 32; then 32 − 6 + 3 = 29. KEY INSIGHT: substitute FIRST, then BODMAS — never mix the two steps. EXAM TRAP: students apply BODMAS to the GIVEN expression with old symbols, then substitute — wrong answer guaranteed. PYQ FREQUENCY: appears 1-2× per year in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC. SHORTCUT: write the converted expression cleanly on rough paper before computing — fewer sign errors. EXAMINER MINDSET: the test isn't arithmetic — it's whether you can hold a substitution rule in working memory while doing real math. CGL & RRB favour 4-symbol redefinitions; SBI PO sometimes uses 5.

(A) 44 is the final answer
(B) 39 alone alone alone alone
(C) 52 alone alone alone alone
(D) 25 alone alone alone alone
cards.back:

Miscellaneous — Substitute: P→÷, Q→×, R→+, S→−. Expression: 36 ÷ 4 × 5 + 7 − 8. BODMAS — ÷ and × left to right (same priority): 36÷4 = 9; 9×5 = 45. Then 45 + 7 − 8 = 44. KEY RULE: when ÷ and × appear consecutively, evaluate LEFT to RIGHT — they have EQUAL precedence. Same for + and −. INSIGHT: many students wrongly apply ÷ FIRST then × (assuming ÷ outranks ×) — both have equal precedence, so order matters. Compute LTR. NUMERICAL TRICK: 36÷4 = 9 instantly recognizable from times-tables; if you panicked on this, drill 12×12 multiplication tables again. EXAM-FAVORITE for SSC CGL Tier 1 (2-3 such Qs per shift). EXAMINER MINDSET: testing operator precedence + substitution discipline — both core programming skills.

If '+' is '−', '−' is '×', '×' is '÷', and '÷' is '+', then 24 ÷ 8 + 6 × 3 − 4 = ?

(A) 24 is the resulting value
(B) 20 alone alone alone alone
(C) 30 alone alone alone alone
(D) 12 alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 24 is the resulting value

Miscellaneous — STEP 1 — substitute: '+' → −, '−' → ×, '×' → ÷, '÷' → +. So 24 ÷ 8 + 6 × 3 − 4 becomes 24 + 8 − 6 ÷ 3 × 4. STEP 2 — apply real BODMAS on the converted expression. ÷ and × together, evaluated LEFT-TO-RIGHT (equal precedence): 6 ÷ 3 = 2; then 2 × 4 = 8. So expression reduces to 24 + 8 − 8 = 24. KEY RULE: ÷ and × have equal precedence and are computed LTR; same for + and −. EXAM TRAP: students isolate 6÷3 alone (= 2), then plug back as 24+8−2 = 30 — that's WRONG because the ×4 must also be processed in the same ÷×-block. CORRECT FLOW: collapse the entire ÷× chain first, then handle +−. PYQ FREQUENCY: this 'compound ÷×' style is a standard CGL/CHSL trap to test BODMAS rigour. EXAMINER MINDSET: verifying you don't 'cherry-pick' operations.

(A) 19 is the resulting value
(B) 11 alone alone alone alone
(C) 27 alone alone alone alone

Miscellaneous — STEP 1 — swap '+' and '×': expression becomes 4 × 5 + 2 − 3. STEP 2 — apply BODMAS on the swapped form: × first → 4×5 = 20. Then 20 + 2 − 3 = 19. KEY METHOD: with a single swap, just rewrite the expression with the two operators exchanged, then compute normally with BODMAS. EXAM TRAP: students apply BODMAS to the ORIGINAL form (4 + 5×2 − 3 = 11) and pick that — wrong because the swap converts the expression. CORRECT SEQUENCE: SWAP first, then BODMAS. INSIGHT: this category trains you for the more advanced 'multi-symbol redefinition' problems where 4-5 operators all change meaning at once.

cards.front:
If 'p × q' means 'p is the father of q', 'p − q' means 'p is the wife of q', and 'p + q' means 'p is the sister of q', then in the relation A × B − C, how is C related to A?

(A) C is the son-in-law of A
(B) C is daughter of A.
(C) C is brother of A.
(D) C is uncle of A (option here)
cards.back:
(A) C is the son-in-law of A

Miscellaneous — DECODE: A × B → A is father of B (so B is A's child). B − C → B is wife of C (so C is B's husband). LINK: B is A's CHILD and B is C's WIFE → B is A's daughter. Therefore C is A's daughter's husband = SON-IN-LAW. KEY METHOD for symbol-relation chains: draw a small family-tree diagram. A → (parent of) B; B ←(wife)← C. Walk the arrows. EXAM TIP: always identify the GENDER from the relation type — 'father' tells you A is male and B can be any child; 'wife' tells you B is female. If B is female AND A's child, B is A's daughter. PYQ ANGLE: blood-relations-via-symbols is a 5-mark category in IBPS PO Prelims. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests ability to chain operators with semantic constraints (gender, parental relation) — useful in graph/relational reasoning.

If 'a # b' means a + b, and 'a @ b' means a × b, find the value of (5 # 3) @ (4 # 2).

(C) 60 alone alone alone alone

Miscellaneous — STEP 1: 5 # 3 = 5 + 3 = 8. STEP 2: 4 # 2 = 4 + 2 = 6. STEP 3: 8 @ 6 = 8 × 6 = 48. KEY METHOD — DEFINE-AND-APPLY: parse innermost parentheses first, then combine outer. Always re-read the operator's definition every time you use it — students lose marks by switching '#' (sum) and '@' (product) mid-solve. EXAM-FAVORITE: SSC, IBPS, RRB all reuse this nested-symbol style — typical 1 Q per Tier 1 paper. SHORTCUT: write the definitions on rough paper as 'a#b = a+b' and 'a@b = a×b' before computing; your eye won't slip back to wrong meanings. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests ability to follow a custom function definition — directly mirrors what you do in programming when calling a user-defined function. INSIGHT: more complex variants use a²+b², a−b², or even a^b — same method, just heavier arithmetic.

cards.front:
If 'P > Q' means 'P is the brother of Q' and 'P × Q' means 'P is the father of Q', then in 'A > B × C', how is A related to C?

(A) Uncle of C (paternal side)
(B) Father of C in this chain
(C) Brother of C close kin
(D) Cousin of C through B
cards.back:
(A) Uncle of C (paternal side)

Miscellaneous — DECODE step-by-step: A > B → A is BROTHER of B. B × C → B is FATHER of C. Chain: A is brother of C's father → A is C's UNCLE (paternal uncle, since B is male = father). KEY METHOD: (1) translate each symbol into the relation. (2) draw a FAMILY TREE on rough paper. Tree: A and B are SIBLINGS (top level); B is parent of C (one level below). So A's relation to C = 'sibling-of-parent' = uncle/aunt. Since B is male (father), A (sibling of male) is the PATERNAL UNCLE if A is male; the symbol said brother → A is male → uncle. WHY NOT 'father'? Because A is B's brother, not C's parent. WHY NOT 'brother'? Because brother requires same-generation; C is one generation below A. WHY NOT 'cousin'? Cousins are children of uncles/aunts, not parent's brother. PYQ FREQUENCY: blood-relations via coded symbols appear in IBPS PO Prelims, SSC CGL Tier 2, RRB NTPC — 1-2 Qs per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests systematic symbol-substitution + family-tree visualization. TIME: ~20-30 seconds with practice.

Miscellaneous — Apply the symbol definitions: 5 @ 3 means '5 is greater than 3' → TRUE (5 > 3). 4 # 9 means '4 is less than 9' → TRUE (4 < 9). Both relations hold, so the combined statement is TRUE. SYMBOLS-FOR-RELATIONS pattern: examiners assign arbitrary symbols to >, <, =, and ask if a chain of relations is consistent. KEY METHOD: substitute back to verify each relation; an entire chain is TRUE only if every link is valid. EXAM PROGRESSION: simpler versions test single relations; harder versions chain 3-4 relations and test transitivity (e.g., A @ B, B @ C → A @ C only if @ is transitive). RELATIONS THAT ARE TRANSITIVE: equality, less-than, greater-than. NOT TRANSITIVE: father-son, friend-of (a friend of a friend isn't necessarily a friend). PYQ FREQUENCY: IBPS Clerk Prelims, RRB NTPC have 2-3 such Qs per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests symbol-decoding + logic — a foundation skill for syllogism.

Miscellaneous — Substitute: '>' → +, '<' → −, '×' → ÷, '÷' → ×. So 16 > 4 < 8 × 2 ÷ 3 becomes 16 + 4 − 8 ÷ 2 × 3. Apply BODMAS strictly: ÷ and × have EQUAL precedence — evaluate LEFT-TO-RIGHT. Step 1: 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Step 2: 4 × 3 = 12. Step 3: 16 + 4 − 12 = 20 − 12 = 8. ANSWER: 8. EXAM TRAP: students who do LTR WITHOUT respecting ÷×-precedence over +− will compute (16+4−8)÷2×3 = 12÷2×3 = 18 (wrong); or (16+4)−8÷2×3 = 20 − 12 = 8 (correct path) but if they mis-bracket they get 20. The distractors 12, 20, 30 each correspond to a SPECIFIC mis-step. KEY METHOD: substitute symbols → write as a clean arithmetic expression → apply BODMAS rigorously (B-O-D-M-A-S; ÷ and × same level, LTR; + and − same level, LTR). PYQ ANGLE: standard SSC CGL/CHSL trap — distractors deliberately match common errors. INSIGHT: 1-mark Q but tests 3-step discipline.

cards.front:
If 'A © B' means A is father of B, 'A * B' means A is brother of B, 'A # B' means A is mother of B, then in P © Q * R, how is P related to R?

(A) Father (P is father of R)
(B) Brother of R alone alone
(C) Uncle of R alone alone
(D) Cannot be determined alone
cards.back:
(A) Father (P is father of R)

Miscellaneous — DECODE: P © Q → P is FATHER of Q. Q * R → Q is BROTHER of R. So Q's father (P) is also R's father, since brothers share parents. Therefore P is FATHER of R. KEY INFERENCE: 'siblings share parents' — if two are siblings, anyone who is parent of one is parent of both. METHOD — DRAW FAMILY TREE: P (top) → Q & R (below, as siblings, both Q and R are children of P). EXAM TIP: when question chains use 'brother/sister', remember they imply same-parent relationship. Distinguish from 'cousin' (one-step further). DOMAIN AWARENESS: real-life half-siblings (different fathers) is an edge case — exam questions assume FULL siblings unless stated. PYQ ANGLE: blood-relations-via-symbols is a 1-2 mark guaranteed Q type in IBPS Clerk Prelims, SBI PO. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests CHAIN INFERENCE + family-tree visualization. TIME: an experienced student solves this in 15-20 seconds.

cards.front:
If '*' means 'subtract', '/' means 'add', '+' means 'multiply', '−' means 'divide', evaluate 10 + 5 / 4 * 3.

(A) 51 is the value
(B) 47 alone alone alone alone
(C) 33 alone alone alone alone
(D) 21 alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 51 is the value

Miscellaneous — Substitute: '*' → −, '/' → +, '+' → ×, '−' → ÷. So 10 + 5 / 4 * 3 becomes 10 × 5 + 4 − 3. BODMAS: × first → 10 × 5 = 50. Then 50 + 4 − 3 = 51. CHECK SIGN-MATCH: '+' in stem becomes ×; '/' becomes +; '*' becomes −. ✓ EXAM TRAP: students confuse the SUBSTITUTION direction (which symbol BECOMES which). Write the swap-table on rough paper. INSIGHT: this 4-symbol redefinition takes ~30 seconds per Q with practice. SHORTCUT: re-write the expression with substitutions BEFORE applying BODMAS — never try to compute and substitute simultaneously. PYQ ANGLE: this question style is a CGL/IBPS staple — 1-2 per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing memory + arithmetic + attention discipline.

cards.front:
If '#' means 'is greater than', '@' means 'is less than', '$' means 'is equal to', then which conclusion follows from: A # B, B @ C, C $ D?

(A) D is greater than B (D # B)
(B) A is less than D alone
(C) C is less than B alone
(D) A is equal to D alone
cards.back:
(A) D is greater than B (D # B)

Miscellaneous — Translate: A # B → A > B. B @ C → B < C, i.e., C > B. C $ D → C = D. SO: D = C > B → D > B → 'D # B' (D is greater than B). VERIFY OTHER OPTIONS: 'A < D'? We have A > B and D > B, but A and D are both greater than B — their relative size is INDETERMINATE. So 'A < D' cannot be concluded. 'C < B'? We have C > B, OPPOSITE. 'A = D'? Indeterminate. KEY METHOD: TRANSITIVITY — if a > b and b < c, you CAN'T directly say a vs c (it depends). But if a > b = c, then a > c. PRACTICE TIP: build a SCALE diagram (number line) with the variables placed; visualize >, <, =. PYQ ANGLE: SSC, IBPS, RBI Grade B routinely include such 3-relation Qs. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests TRANSITIVITY of relations and the ability to identify when conclusions are SOUND vs INDETERMINATE.
cards.option1: A is less than D alone
cards.option2: C is less than B alone
cards.option3: A is equal to D alone

cards.front:
If '@' means '+', '*' means '×', '$' means '−', and '%' means '÷', evaluate: 36 % 6 * 2 @ 5 $ 1.

(A) 16 is the value
(B) 10 alone alone alone alone
(C) 30 alone alone alone alone
(D) 8 alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 16 is the value

Miscellaneous — Substitute: '@' → +, '*' → ×, '$' → −, '%' → ÷. Expression: 36 ÷ 6 × 2 + 5 − 1. BODMAS — ÷ and × LTR: 36 ÷ 6 = 6; 6 × 2 = 12. Then 12 + 5 − 1 = 16. KEY RULE: when ÷ and × appear together, evaluate LEFT-TO-RIGHT (equal precedence) — students often mistakenly do × before ÷, getting wrong answers. SAME LTR rule applies to + and −. CHECKLIST: (1) substitute symbols. (2) identify ÷× block, evaluate LTR. (3) handle +− last, also LTR. PYQ FREQUENCY: appears 2-3× per CGL Tier 1 paper. INSIGHT: this category is essentially BODMAS-revision under symbol-disguise — disciplined students see through the disguise instantly. EXAM TIP: in test conditions, write 'swap-table' (e.g., '@=+, *=×, $=−, %=÷') on rough paper before plugging — saves 30+ seconds per Q.
